passages.locator: Field guide PDF page 3, master page 16
passages.text: Question a judge asks Chapter B1. Combustion, from zero Must say Fire is a fast chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases heat and light. For a hydrocarbon fuel, the overall result is carbon dioxide, water and heat. The heat keeps the reaction going by heating more fuel. That loop (heat makes fuel vapour, fuel vapour burns, burning makes heat) is what a fire is. The fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and heat. Remove any one and the fire stops. Every fire-safety measure attacks one side: choose materials that resist burning (fuel), control oxygen (oxygen), keep ignition sources away and cool the fire (heat). Should know Solids don’t burn directly. A solid like fabric or plastic is first heated until it breaks down and gives off flammable gases (this is called pyrolysis). Those gases burn in the air just above the surface. The flame’s heat then reaches the solid and makes more gas. So “flame spread” over a solid is really a race: can the flame heat the solid ahead of it fast enough to keep feeding itself?

passages.text: Two kinds of flame: Type How it works Example Premixed Fuel and air are mixed before burning A gas stove’s blue ring Diffusion Fuel and air meet only at the flame; the flame lives where they mix A candle, a burning fabric, almost every accidental fire Accidental fires in spacecraft are diffusion flames. That’s why the supply of oxygen to the flame, which depends on airflow and gravity, matters so much. Flame colour: yellow-orange light comes from glowing soot particles; blue light comes from excited molecules in the reaction zone. Microgravity flames are often dimmer and bluer because soot forms and behaves differently there (B2). Ignition: a material ignites when enough of it is heated to give off flammable gas at a high enough rate, in contact with oxygen, near a heat source. Extinction: a flame goes out when it loses heat faster than the reaction produces it, or when oxygen or fuel can’t reach the reaction zone fast enough.

passages.text: Deep: the “race” in one idea (the Damköhler number) Two times compete in every flame: how long the gas spends in the hot zone (the residence time) and how long the chemistry needs to react (the reaction time). Their ratio is called the Damköhler number. If gas rushes through too fast (strong airflow), the chemistry can’t keep up and the flame is blown off. If gas barely moves (very weak airflow), not enough oxygen arrives and heat losses by radiation win, so the flame quenches. Between those extremes is where a fire burns most easily. Section B2 turns this into the most important picture in this guide. Say it in one line: “Fire is a loop of heat, fuel vapour and oxygen; break the loop and the fire goes out.” B2. Gravity and flames Must say On Earth, hot gas rises. It’s lighter than the cool air around it. As it rises, it pulls fresh air in at the bottom of the flame. This flow, driven by gravity, is called buoyant flow. It’s why a candle flame is a teardrop pointing up, and why upward burning is usually fastest on Earth. In orbit there is no buoyancy. Hot gas doesn’t rise. Oxygen reaches the flame only by slow diffusion, or by whatever air the ventilation fans push.

passages.text: The challenge page describes a candle flame in microgravity: it “becomes a ghostly blue sphere reliant on diffusion for its oxygen.” On the Moon and Mars there’s a little buoyancy: less than Earth, more than orbit. You might expect fires there to be “in between”. NASA’s lunar-gravity tests found that for some materials the Moon can be worse than both. Here’s why. Must say: the flammability map (the U-curve) Imagine plotting, for one material, the lowest oxygen level at which it can keep burning against the speed of the air flowing past it: Airflow What happens The limit Almost none Too little oxygen arrives; radiation carries heat away; the flame starves (quenching) Needs a lot of oxygen to survive Gentle Oxygen arrives steadily, the flame stays hot Lowest: the material burns most easily Strong Gas rushes through before it can react; the flame is blown off (blowoff) Needs more oxygen again So the limit forms a U-shape against airflow. The bottom of the U is the most dangerous airflow: the one where the material burns at the lowest oxygen.

passages.text: Place Typical airflow past a burning sample Where on the U Moon Weaker buoyant flow than Earth Possibly close to the bottom That’s the whole scientific reason the Moon worries NASA, and why Olson and colleagues (2024, Fire Safety Journal) describe lunar gravity as near the minimum of the oxygen–gravity flammability boundary (our paraphrase; do not present it as a quotation). Should know: how strong is lunar buoyant flow? A common textbook scaling says the buoyant flow speed grows like the cube root of gravity: speed ∝ g^(1/3). This is a rough estimate, not a measurement. ICES-2025-392 says plainly that the lunar gravity velocity “is not known” (p10). Place Gravity (Earth = 1) g^(1/3) If 1 g ≈ 35 cm/s, rough estimate Earth 1 1.00 35 cm/s Mars 0.38 0.72 about 25 cm/s Moon 0.165 0.55 about 19 cm/s Orbit ≈ 0 ≈ 0 only fan-driven flow Use it only to explain the idea: the Moon’s natural airflow past a fire is about half of Earth’s, which may sit nearer the bottom of the U.

passages.text: Should know: flame spread words Term Meaning Opposed flow Air moves against the direction the flame spreads (like downward burning on Earth); usually slower spread Concurrent flow Air moves the same way the flame spreads (like upward burning); usually faster, more dangerous Thermally thin fuel Thin enough to heat through quickly (paper, thin fabric, thin PMMA film) Thermally thick fuel Thick enough that only the surface heats (a PMMA block) Deep: why microgravity flames look different Without buoyancy, the flame’s hot products don’t sweep away. Flames get larger and rounder; soot can form differently and burn out or escape; radiation becomes a larger share of heat loss. That’s why microgravity flames can be dim, blue and spherical, and why radiation drives quenching at very low flow. Deep: imitating gravity with electricity ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment used electric fields acting on the ions that occur naturally in flames to push the flame like a body force. The challenge page notes that “partial gravity was mimicked” this way. It’s a clever lab trick, not a substitute for real lunar gravity. Say it in one line: “Fire burns most easily in a gentle breeze, and the Moon’s weak gravity may give fires exactly that breeze.” Master Document 1.0 · Team Code Blooded · page 18

passages.text: B3. Oxygen, pressure and habitat atmospheres Must say Earth’s air is about 21% oxygen and 78% nitrogen at 14.7 psi (101 kPa) at sea level. Why a Moon base changes the air: spacesuits are kept at low pressure so they stay flexible. The challenge page says suits are “filled with 100% oxygen to only 4.3 psi”. Going from Earth-pressure air into a 4.3 psi suit can cause the bends (decompression sickness), because nitrogen dissolved in the body forms bubbles. So astronauts “pre-breathe” pure oxygen first. To make moonwalks quick and frequent, NASA plans habitats at lower pressure and higher oxygen fraction, between a suit and Earth’s air. Atmosphere Pressure Oxygen Source Earth, sea level 14.7 psi ~21% Standard Moon base, challenge page “10.2 psi or less” “30% or greater” Flame in Freefall challenge Moon (FM² / lunar lander) 8.2 psia ~34% (control bands up to 37%) FM² briefing [9] Spacesuit 4.3 psi 100% Challenge page Must say: why more oxygen fraction is more dangerous, even when you can breathe normally What your lungs care about is the partial pressure of oxygen: total pressure × oxygen fraction.

passages.text: Atmosphere Oxygen partial pressure Earth: 14.7 × 0.21 ≈ 3.1 psi (21 kPa) Moon base: 8.2 × 0.34 ≈ 2.8 psi (19 kPa), roughly what you’d breathe at about 800 m altitude So astronauts breathe almost normally. But a flame cares about something else: how much non- burning gas (nitrogen) surrounds it. Nitrogen soaks up heat and cools the flame. At 34% oxygen there’s much less nitrogen per unit of oxygen, so flames run hotter and more materials can keep burning. That’s why NASA finds materials more flammable at reduced pressure and raised oxygen fraction, and why the challenge page says this means “more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable.” Should know: a short history of spacecraft air Programme Cabin atmosphere (approximate) What it taught Apollo 1 ground test, 1967 100% oxygen, above sea-level pressure A fire spread through the cabin in seconds; three astronauts died.

passages.text: K2. Ten misconceptions to correct politely Misconception Correction “Fire cannot burn in space.” It can; it looks and behaves differently. “Less gravity always means weaker fires.” Not always: a gentle airflow can make some materials burn at lower oxygen. “The Moon is more flammable.” For three of five tested materials, yes; for two, no. “Table 2 gives lunar limits.” It is NASA’s conservative margin, not a measurement. “High oxygen means astronauts get too much oxygen.” The partial pressure stays near Earth’s; it is the fire risk that rises. “SI wrote the project.” SI tools drafted and coded under direction; the team designed, checked and decided, and lists every tool. “The forecast is a guess.” It is a stated model, sealed and scored. It can lose. “No flame means the fire is out.” Cool flames and smouldering exist. “Turning off fans always starves a fire.” Under partial gravity, buoyancy still moves air. “NASA changed its test.” ICES-2025-392 is evidence, not a change to the standard. K3. Check the forecast’s seal yourself Anyone can do this in two minutes. It was done independently while preparing this document, and it passed. cd dist/forecast-lock # 1. Fingerprint the file. Expect: # 9f565bc7195936bde5faff67841c5e1e6537581bc4fc560018838fbf996a8fa3 sha256sum fm2-v1.json # 2.

Verify the signature against trusted authorities openssl ts -verify -data fm2-v1.json -in fm2-v1.tsr \ -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt Step What we saw 1 The fingerprint matches 2 “Time stamp: Nov 14 12:57:06 2026 GMT”, hash algorithm SHA-256, and the same fingerprint as the message data 3 “Verification: OK” What this proves: that exactly this file existed at that moment. What it does not prove: who made it, or that it is right. Change one character of the file and step 1 gives a different fingerprint and step 3 fails. K4.
